Git, from absolute zero

You keep hearing "just push it to GitHub" as if everyone was born knowing what that means. Nobody was. This guide assumes you know nothing: not what a terminal is, not what a commit is. By the last stop you will be branching, fixing merge conflicts and opening pull requests without breaking a sweat.

How this guide works

It is drawn like a metro map. Every chapter is a stop, and the stops are grouped into colored lines. Ride them in order the first time. Later, jump around with the route map on the left or the search box (Ctrl + K, or just /).

  • AFoundationsThe terminal, what git is, installing it.
  • BEveryday gitSaving snapshots, reading history, ignoring junk.
  • CBranchingParallel versions, merging them back, surviving conflicts.
  • DGitHubPushing, pulling, logging in, pull requests, forks and the website itself.
  • ERescue and habitsUndoing mistakes, handy tools, working like a professional.
  • FTerminusA final challenge, a sandbox, a cheat sheet and a glossary.

You cannot break anything here

Most stops have a practice terminal: a pretend command line running a simulated git, right inside this page. It never touches your real computer, so type whatever you like, make mistakes on purpose, and hit Reset when things get weird.

Practice terminals come with missions, short step-by-step goals that tick themselves off as you go. Stuck? Every step has a hint, and the buttons under each terminal type example commands for you (you still press Enter yourself, so you see what happens).

Words with a dotted underline, like repository or commit, show a short definition when you hover or tap them. They all live in the glossary too.

Why does git even exist?

Picture writing a school essay. You save it. Then you want to make big changes but keep the old version, so you "Save As" a copy. Then another. A week later your folder looks like the left side below. Click the button a few times.

Now picture five people editing the same files on different computers all week. That is the problem git solves. It remembers every version of every file, who changed what and why, and it lets several people work on the same project and combine their work safely.

What you will be able to do

  • Use the terminal without fear
  • Save your work as commits and travel back to any of them
  • Try ideas on branches without breaking the working version
  • Merge branches and calmly fix merge conflicts
  • Put a project on GitHub, then push and pull changes
  • Open, review and merge pull requests the way real teams do
  • Undo almost any mistake, and know which undos are dangerous

Reading everything and doing every mission takes a few hours. You do not have to do it in one sitting: the page remembers which stops you have visited. That memory stays in this browser; nothing is sent anywhere.

What is the main job of git?

Right. Git is a history recorder for a folder of files. Putting things online is what sites like GitHub add on top.

The terminal, without the panic

Git lives in the terminal: the dark window where movie hackers type very fast. It looks intimidating, but it is just a very literal way of talking to your computer. Ten minutes here makes everything after it easy.

What it is

Normally you control your computer by pointing and clicking: double-click a folder to open it, drag a file to the trash. The terminal does the same jobs with typed commands. You type a command, press Enter, the computer does it and prints a reply.

Clicking

Double-click "Documents".
Right-click, New Folder, type "recipes".

Typing

cd Documents
mkdir recipes

Why bother? Typing is exact, fast and repeatable, and git was built for it. Every git tutorial, error message and forum answer speaks in commands. Learn this language and all of that becomes readable.

Terminal, command line, console and shell get used interchangeably. Strictly speaking, the terminal is the window and the shell is the program inside it that understands your commands (bash, zsh, PowerShell). You can ignore the difference for now.

Opening one

Install git first (the Install and set up stop shows how). It comes with Git Bash, a terminal that understands the same commands as Mac and Linux. Open the Start menu, type Git Bash, and open it. Use Git Bash for everything in this guide.

Windows also has PowerShell and Command Prompt. Git works in them, but some basic commands differ (Command Prompt uses dir instead of ls, for example), which is confusing while you are learning.

Bonus: in VS Code, Terminal, New Terminal opens one inside your editor. Pick "Git Bash" from the small dropdown next to the plus button.

Press Cmd + Space, type Terminal, press Enter. That is it. It runs a shell called zsh, which understands every command in this guide.

Bonus: in VS Code, Terminal, New Terminal opens one inside your editor.

Press Ctrl + Alt + T on most distributions, or search your apps for Terminal. You are most likely running bash, which understands everything here.

Reading the prompt

When the terminal is ready for you, it shows a prompt. Here is a typical one. Hover or tap the colored parts.

you@laptop ~/projects (main) $

Hover or tap a part of the prompt.

Tutorials (this one included) write commands as $ git status. The $ only marks "this is a command". Type just git status.

Anatomy of a command

Every command follows the same grammar: a program name, sometimes a subcommand, then options and arguments, separated by spaces.

git commit -m "Fix typo in the menu"

Hover or tap a part of the command.

A few more so the pattern sticks: ls -a is a program and a flag. cd Documents is a program and an argument. git push -u origin main is a program, a subcommand, a flag and two arguments.

Folders and paths

Files live in a tree of folders, which the terminal calls directories. A path gives directions through that tree, with / between names: ~/projects/recipes/pancakes.txt means "in my home folder, then projects, then recipes, the file pancakes.txt".

SymbolMeans
~Your home folder, like /home/you or C:/Users/you
.The folder you are in right now
..The folder one level up (the parent)
/At the start of a path, the very top of the drive. In the middle, a separator between names.

A path starting with / or ~ is absolute and works from anywhere. Anything else is relative to your current directory: cd recipes only works if a recipes folder exists right where you are standing.

The commands you actually need

pwd
Print working directory: which folder am I in?
ls
List the files and folders here. ls -a also shows hidden ones, whose names start with a dot (like .git).
cd folder
Change directory: walk into a folder. cd .. goes up a level, cd ~ (or plain cd) goes home.
mkdir name
Make a new directory.
touch notes.txt
Create an empty file (Git Bash, macOS and Linux).
cat notes.txt
Print a file's contents on the screen.
echo "text"
Print some text. With > the text goes into a file instead: echo "hello" > notes.txt creates or overwrites notes.txt. >> adds to the end.
rm notes.txt
Delete a file. There is no recycle bin. rm -r folder deletes a folder and everything in it.
clear
Wipe the screen. Nothing is undone, it just clears the clutter. Ctrl + L does the same.

Practice

This terminal runs a pretend computer inside the page. The panel on the right shows its folders the way a file explorer would, so you can watch your commands take effect. Follow the mission.

Keyboard tricks that save hours

  • Tab finishes names for you. Type cd Doc and press Tab. If several names fit, it shows the options. This works in the practice terminal too.
  • Up and Down bring back commands you already ran. No retyping.
  • Ctrl + C cancels whatever is running, or the line you are typing. In most terminals it does not copy.
  • Copy and paste: in Git Bash, right-click (or Ctrl + Insert and Shift + Insert). On macOS, the usual Cmd + C and Cmd + V. On Linux, Ctrl + Shift + C and Ctrl + Shift + V.
  • Names with spaces need quotes: cd "My Documents". Simpler: never put spaces in project names. Use dashes, like my-project.

Many commands print nothing at all when they succeed. If you get the prompt back without an error, it worked.

You are in ~/projects/recipes. Which command takes you to ~/projects?

Right. .. always means one level up. cd projects would look for a folder called projects inside recipes, and pwd only tells you where you are.

A tutorial says: $ git status. What do you type?

Right. The dollar sign is the prompt, printed by the terminal. You type what comes after it.

What git actually is

Git is a time machine for a folder. It takes snapshots of your files when you ask, keeps every one of them, and lets many people add their own snapshots to the same project without trampling each other.

Version control in one sentence

Version control means keeping track of every change to a set of files over time, so you can see who changed what, when and why, and return to any earlier state. Git is the version control system nearly everyone uses, from solo hobby projects to Linux, Windows and most of the software you touch every day. Linus Torvalds wrote it in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel, and it is free and open source.

Snapshots, not save files

When you tell git "remember this", it takes a snapshot of the whole project and files it away with a short description. That saved snapshot is called a commit. Commits line up one after another into a history, like stations on a line. Drag the slider or click the stations to travel through the history of one recipe:

Green lines were added in that commit, red lines removed. You can see who made each change and the reason they gave. A git history gives you exactly that, for every file in the project.

No. Git is clever about storage: files that did not change between snapshots are not stored again, and everything is compressed. A project with thousands of commits usually has only a few megabytes of history.

Git and GitHub are different things

This trips up everyone. Git is a program on your computer, and it works entirely offline. GitHub is a website (owned by Microsoft) that stores copies of git projects online and adds teamwork features on top: pull requests, code review, issues, automation.

Git

  • A program you install
  • Works offline, on your computer
  • Tracks history, branches and merges
  • Free and open source

GitHub

  • A website, github.com
  • Stores copies of repositories online
  • Adds pull requests, issues, code review, automation
  • Alternatives: GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg

Git is your camera and photo album. GitHub is a shared online album where the whole team uploads photos, comments on them and decides which ones make the final cut.

A little vocabulary before we start

repository
A project folder that git tracks, usually shortened to "repo". Its history lives in a hidden folder called .git inside it.
commit
One saved snapshot, with a message.
branch
A separate line of commits, for working on something without disturbing the rest.
remote
A copy of the repository somewhere else, usually on GitHub.
push / pull
Upload your new commits to a remote, or download other people's.

Each gets its own stop later. No need to memorize anything now.

What git is not good at

  • Huge binary files like videos, Photoshop files or game assets. Git keeps every version of every file, so a 2 GB video edited ten times becomes 20 GB of history. Git LFS exists for that.
  • Live co-editing like Google Docs. Git combines work in deliberate steps, not keystroke by keystroke.
  • Backing up your whole computer. It is built for projects, not for your photo library.

You are on a plane with no internet. Can you still make commits?

Right. Commits are saved in the .git folder on your own disk. You only need the internet to push them to GitHub later.

Install git and introduce yourself

A few minutes of setup you only ever do once per computer: install git, tell it your name, and pick sensible defaults.

Install it

  1. Download Git for Windows from git-scm.com/downloads and run the installer.
  2. Click Next through almost everything. The defaults are good. Two screens are worth changing:
  3. "Choosing the default editor": pick Visual Studio Code (or Notepad) instead of Vim. Git opens this editor whenever it needs you to type a message, and Vim is famously hard to exit.
  4. "Adjusting the name of the initial branch": choose "Override the default branch name" and type main.
  5. Open Git Bash from the Start menu when it finishes.

The installer also sets up Git Credential Manager, which handles logging in to GitHub later. Keep it.

macOS often has git already, bundled with Apple's developer tools. Open Terminal and run:

$ git --version

A version number means you are done. If instead a window offers to install the command line developer tools, click Install and wait. That gives you git.

Want a newer version? With Homebrew installed: brew install git.

Use your package manager:

# Ubuntu, Debian, Mint
$ sudo apt update
$ sudo apt install git
# Fedora
$ sudo dnf install git
# Arch
$ sudo pacman -S git

Check that it worked. Any version from the last few years is fine:

$ git --version
git version 2.51.0

Tell git who you are

Every commit is stamped with an author name and email. Git refuses to commit until they are set, so do it now:

$ git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
$ git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
  • --global means "for every repository on this computer". The settings go into a file called .gitconfig in your home folder.
  • Use the same email as your GitHub account, so GitHub can link your commits to your profile.
  • Rather keep your email private? GitHub gives you a no-reply address under Settings, Emails. It looks like 12345+you@users.noreply.github.com, and you can use it here instead.

Defaults worth setting

init.defaultBranch main
New projects start on a branch called main, matching GitHub. Without it, git uses master and prints a long warning.
core.editor
The editor git opens when it wants you to type something, like a commit message. "code --wait" makes that VS Code.
pull.rebase false
What git pull does when both you and GitHub have new work: merge them, the beginner-friendly choice. Without it, git stops and asks. The GitHub stops explain why.
core.autocrlf
Windows ends lines of text differently from macOS and Linux. true on Windows and input elsewhere stops files from looking "changed" when they are not.

Practice on a fresh install

This pretend computer just installed git and has none of these settings. Try git config --list before and after.

Get a decent code editor

You will edit files constantly. Visual Studio Code is free, runs everywhere and has git built in: changed files are colored in the sidebar, and there are buttons for staging, committing and resolving conflicts. Everything you learn here maps directly onto those buttons.

Graphical git apps are fine, and plenty of professionals use them daily. But they hide what is happening underneath. Learn the commands first; after that, any app is just buttons for things you already understand.

What does --global mean in git config --global user.name "Ada"?

Right. Global settings live in ~/.gitconfig and apply to all your repositories. Without --global, a setting applies only to the repository you are in.

Your first repository

Enough theory. Let's make a project, put it under git and save the first snapshot. This is the loop you will repeat for the rest of your life: change something, stage it, commit it.

Step 1: a folder

A repository starts life as a completely normal folder:

$ mkdir recipes
$ cd recipes

Step 2: git init

$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/you/recipes/.git/

That is all it takes. Git created a hidden folder called .git inside recipes. That hidden folder is the repository: every commit, branch and setting lives there. Your own files stay exactly where they are.

$ ls -a
./   ../   .git/

Never edit or delete the .git folder by hand. Deleting it deletes the entire history of the project. Your current files survive, but every commit is gone.

Do not run git init in your home folder or on your Desktop, or git will try to track everything in there. Always cd into a project folder first. If it already happened, deleting that stray .git folder (only that one) fixes it.

Step 3: make a file

Create a file any way you like: in VS Code, in Notepad, or straight from the terminal:

$ echo "Pancakes: flour, eggs, milk" > pancakes.txt

Step 4: git status, your best friend

git status tells you what git sees right now. Run it constantly. It costs nothing and it explains itself. Hover the parts of its answer:

On branch main No commits yet Untracked files: (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed) pancakes.txt nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

Hover or tap each colored part of the output.

Step 5: git add

Committing is a two-step dance. First you pick which changes go into the next snapshot. That is called staging, and git add does it:

$ git add pancakes.txt
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
        new file:   pancakes.txt

In a real terminal that line turns green: the file is staged and ready for the snapshot. Why two steps? That is the whole next stop.

Step 6: git commit

$ git commit -m "Add pancake recipe"
[main (root-commit) dc90184] Add pancake recipe
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 pancakes.txt

Your first commit. Reading the reply: it went onto the branch main, it is the root (very first) commit, its ID starts with dc90184, and it added one file containing one line. The text after -m is the commit message.

Without -m, git opens your text editor and waits for you to write a message, save and close it. If it opened Vim and you feel trapped: press Esc, type :wq, press Enter.

Step 7: look at your history

$ git log
commit dc90184a7a70b49d29b3a36fb05a03298be8832c (HEAD -> main)
Author: Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>
Date:   Mon Sep 14 09:15:53 2026 +0000

    Add pancake recipe

From here on, the rhythm is always the same:

Do it yourself

The panels show where your changes are (explained on the next stop) and your history drawn as a line. Watch a station appear when you commit.

A decent commit message

Future you will read these messages when something breaks. Make them useful:

  • Say specifically what changed: "Add pancake recipe", not "update".
  • Write it as a command, the way git's own messages read: "Add", "Fix", "Remove", not "Added" or "Adding".
  • Keep the first line short, around 50 characters. More detail can go in a second paragraph.

The Good habits stop has a checker that grades your messages as you type.

You just ran git add notes.txt. Is notes.txt saved in the history yet?

Right. git add puts the change in the staging area. git commit is what records a snapshot. Pushing is a separate, later step that uploads commits.

What does git init create?

Right. It turns the folder into a repository by adding .git. Nothing is saved until your first commit, and nothing goes online.

The three areas (the big idea)

If git ever confuses you, it is almost always about this. Your changes live in one of three places, and nearly every everyday command just moves them between those places.

Where changes live

  1. Working directory The real files in your project folder, the ones you open and edit. Git notices changes but saves nothing automatically.
  2. Staging area (also called the index) A draft of your next commit. git add copies a change here. Stage one file, a few, or everything.
  3. Repository The permanent history inside .git. git commit takes whatever is staged and saves it as a new snapshot.

Think of a train station. Your working directory is the city, where passengers (your changes) wander around. The staging area is the platform: only the passengers you send there will board. git commit is the train leaving: everyone on the platform travels together, and the departure goes into the timetable forever. Passengers still in the city simply wait for a later train.

Why have a staging area at all?

Because you rarely change just one thing. Say you fixed a typo and also started on a new feature. You want two separate commits, "Fix typo" and "Add search", so either can be understood or undone on its own. Staging lets you put only the typo fix on the platform, commit it, then deal with the rest.

Click through it

Press Edit on a file to change it, Stage to move the change onto the platform, then write a message and Commit. The dark box at the bottom shows the actual git commands your clicks correspond to.

The life of a file

Every file is in one of these states. git status is just a report of which files are where.

The commands

CommandWhat it does
git add file.txtStage one file
git add .Stage every change in this folder and below: new, modified and deleted files
git add -pWalk through your changes chunk by chunk and choose which to stage
git restore --staged file.txtUnstage it. Your edit stays in the file.
git restore file.txtThrow your edit away and put back the last committed (or staged) version
git commit -am "..."Shortcut: stage all modified tracked files and commit. Brand-new files are not included.
git diffShow changes you have not staged yet
git diff --stagedShow what is staged, which is exactly what the next commit will contain

git restore file.txt overwrites your file with the last saved version. Edits you never committed are gone, with no undo. Not sure? Use git stash instead (see power tools).

Practice

You changed two files but want to commit only one of them. What do you do?

Right. Only staged changes go into a commit. The other file stays modified in your working directory, ready for a later commit.

git diff prints nothing, but git status lists "Changes to be committed". Why?

Right. Use git diff --staged to see staged changes. This confuses everyone at least once.

Reading history

A history is only useful if you can read it. Learn to list commits, open one up, compare versions, and step back in time to look around.

git log

$ git log
commit 7ccb74ce66d73f1a89766c7ef7a3c9810db31af2 (HEAD -> main)
Author: Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com>
Date:   Tue Sep 15 10:07:38 2026 +0000

    Add guacamole recipe

commit f4ee3e34ec6c1269719ea7c2d8c20b788caac512
Author: Sam <sam@example.com>
Date:   Tue Sep 15 09:21:52 2026 +0000

    Add salt to pancakes

Newest first. When the list is longer than your screen, git shows it in a scrollable viewer: arrow keys and space scroll, and q gets you out. (Everyone gets stuck in there once. Now you know.)

Most of the time you want the short version:

$ git log --oneline
7ccb74c (HEAD -> main) Add guacamole recipe
f4ee3e3 Add salt to pancakes
2a4cc3a Add salsa recipe
dc90184 Add pancake recipe
3f1b2c0 Start the recipe book

And to see every branch drawn as a graph: git log --oneline --graph --all. The practice terminals draw that graph for you as a metro map instead.

Hashes: every commit's ID

That jumble like 7ccb74ce66d7... is the commit's hash, a unique ID git calculates from the commit's contents, author, time and parent. Change anything and the hash changes, which is how git can tell history was not tampered with.

You never need all 40 characters. The first 7 are enough to point at a commit: git show 7ccb74c.

HEAD: you are here

HEAD is git's name for "the commit you are on right now". Usually it points at a branch (HEAD -> main in the log), and the branch points at its newest commit. In the graphs in this guide, HEAD is the black label and the spinning ring around a station.

You can count backwards from it:

HEAD
the current commit
HEAD~1
one commit before it (also written HEAD^)
HEAD~3
three commits back

Looking inside a commit

$ git show f4ee3e3

prints the commit's details plus a diff: exactly which lines changed. Diffs look scary but have a simple structure. Hover the parts:

diff --git a/pancakes.txt b/pancakes.txt index 3b18e51..6f8a38c 100644 --- a/pancakes.txt +++ b/pancakes.txt @@ -2,3 +2,4 @@ - 2 cups flour - 2 eggs - 1 cup milk + - 1 pinch of salt

Hover or tap each part of the diff.

Comparing versions with git diff

git diff
Changes in your files that are not staged yet
git diff --staged
Staged changes: exactly what your next commit will contain
git diff HEAD~2
Everything that changed since two commits ago
git diff main feature
The difference between two branches

Run git diff --staged right before every commit. It is the cheapest code review you will ever get: you will catch leftover debug lines and files you did not mean to include.

Time travel

You can move HEAD to an old commit and see the project exactly as it was then. Your files change to match that moment, and nothing is lost: the newer commits are still there.

This state is called detached HEAD: HEAD points at a commit instead of a branch. It sounds alarming but it is just sightseeing mode. Look around, then go back with git switch main. Want to keep working from that old point? Put a branch there: git switch -c idea-from-the-past.

Practice

Handy history commands

git log -p file.txt
Every change ever made to one file, with diffs
git log --author="Sam"
Only one person's commits
git log --grep="salsa"
Commits whose message mentions a word
git log -n 5
Only the five newest commits
git blame file.txt
Who last changed each line (see power tools)

What does HEAD~1 mean?

Right. ~1 means one step back from HEAD, ~2 two steps, and so on.

In a diff, what does a line starting with - mean?

Right. - removed, + added, a leading space means unchanged context.

Ignoring files with .gitignore

Some files should never end up in history: passwords, gigabytes of downloaded libraries, logs, your computer's junk files. A small text file called .gitignore keeps them out.

What should never be committed

Secrets

.env files, API keys, passwords, private keys. Once pushed to GitHub, assume they are stolen.

Things you can regenerate

Downloaded libraries (node_modules/, venv/), build output (dist/, build/), caches (__pycache__/).

Personal junk

macOS .DS_Store, Windows Thumbs.db, editor folders like .idea/, and *.log files.

Huge files

Videos, datasets, zip archives. They bloat history forever, even after you delete them.

How it works

Create a file named exactly .gitignore (with the leading dot, no extension) in the top folder of your repository. Each line is a pattern. Git then pretends matching untracked files do not exist: they vanish from git status, and git add . skips them.

.gitignore
# secrets
.env

# dependencies and build output
node_modules/
dist/

# logs and OS junk
*.log
.DS_Store

Commit the .gitignore file itself, so everyone working on the project gets the same rules.

Pattern rules

PatternIgnores
secret.txtAnything named secret.txt, in any folder
*.logEvery file ending in .log, anywhere. * matches any characters except a slash.
build/Folders named build, and everything inside. The trailing slash means "folders only".
/buildOnly the build at the top of the repository, not src/build. A leading slash anchors the pattern.
docs/*.pdfPDFs directly inside the top-level docs folder. A slash in the middle also anchors the pattern.
**/temptemp at any depth. ** matches any number of folders.
!keep.logAn exception: do not ignore keep.log, even though *.log said so
# noteNothing. Lines starting with # are comments for humans.

Test the rules

Edit either box. The right column explains every decision, including files ignored only because a folder they sit in is ignored.

An exception cannot rescue a file inside a folder that is ignored as a whole. If logs/ is ignored, !logs/keep.log does nothing, because git never even looks inside logs. Ignore logs/* instead (the contents, not the folder), and the exception works. Try both in the tester.

Already committed? .gitignore will not help

.gitignore only affects files git is not tracking yet. If a file was already committed, adding it to .gitignore changes nothing: git keeps tracking it. Untrack it first:

$ echo ".env" >> .gitignore
$ git rm --cached .env
rm '.env'
$ git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"

--cached means "remove it from git, but leave the real file on my disk".

Removing it now does not remove it from history; anyone can still open the old commit. And bots scan GitHub for leaked keys within minutes. Revoke or rotate the key first: create a new one on that service and disable the old one. That is the actual fix. Scrubbing history is optional cleanup afterwards.

Do not write it from scratch

GitHub keeps ready-made templates for nearly every language and tool at github.com/github/gitignore, and offers them in a dropdown when you create a repository on the website. Start from one of those and add your own lines.

Practice

You add passwords.txt to .gitignore, but it was committed last week. What happens?

Right. Ignore rules only apply to untracked files. And if that file was ever pushed, change those passwords.

Branches: parallel lines

Branches let you try an idea on the side while the main version stays safe. Draw git history and it looks exactly like a metro map; a branch is simply a new line splitting off.

Why branch?

Say your recipe site works. You want to redesign the layout, which will take a few days and break things along the way. Meanwhile someone reports a typo that needs fixing today. Without branches, the half-finished redesign and the typo fix get tangled together. With branches, the redesign lives on its own line, and main stays clean and working the whole time.

What a branch really is

The part most people get wrong: a branch is not a copy of your files. It is a lightweight label, a sticky note with a name on it, pointing at one commit. Creating one is instant and costs nothing.

When you commit, git makes the new commit and moves the label of the branch you are on forward onto it. HEAD is how git knows which label that is.

The commands

git branch
List branches. The one marked * is where you are.
git branch name
Create a branch at the current commit, but stay where you are.
git switch name
Move onto a branch. Your files change to match it.
git switch -c name
Create a branch and switch to it in one go. The one you will use most.
git switch -
Jump back to the branch you were on before.
git branch -m new-name
Rename the current branch.
git branch -d name
Delete a branch that has been merged. -D forces it even if it has not. Careful.

Older tutorials use git checkout name and git checkout -b name. Those still work fine. git switch arrived in 2019 because checkout did too many unrelated jobs. Same result, clearer name.

Switching changes your files

When you switch branches, git rewrites the files in your folder to match the commit that branch points at. Files that only exist on the other branch disappear from your folder (they are safe in history) and come back when you switch back. It feels like a magic trick the first time. You will see it in the mission below.

If you have uncommitted edits, git carries them over to the new branch when that is safe. If switching would overwrite them, git refuses with "Your local changes would be overwritten". Commit the work, or stash it, then switch.

Practice

Naming branches

  • Describe the work: add-dark-mode, fix-login-crash, update-readme.
  • Lowercase words joined by dashes. Spaces are not allowed.
  • Many teams use prefixes like feature/search or fix/menu-typo. Slashes are allowed.

You create a branch called experiment. What does git copy?

Right. That is why branches are so cheap that people create them for every small task.

You are on main and run git branch feature. Which branch are you on now?

Right. git branch name only creates the label. git switch -c name creates it and moves you onto it.

Merging lines back together

A branch is only useful if its work can come back. Merging takes the commits from one branch and brings them into another.

The one rule to remember

You always merge into the branch you are on. To bring feature into main: go to main first, then merge feature.

$ git switch main
$ git merge feature

Depending on what happened on each branch, git merges in one of two ways.

Fast-forward: main did not move

If main got no new commits since the branch split off, there is nothing to combine. Git just slides the main label forward to where feature is. That is a fast-forward. Run the steps and watch the main label.

Three-way merge: both moved

If both branches got new commits, git combines them. It compares three versions (the two branch tips and the commit where they split, hence "three-way") and works out the combined result. It records that in a new merge commit with two parents. On the map it is an interchange station.

In a real terminal, git opens your editor with a ready-made message like Merge branch 'feature' for the merge commit. Just save and close it. The practice terminal fills it in for you.

After merging: delete the branch

Once merged, the branch label has done its job:

$ git branch -d feature
Deleted branch feature (was 469aa30).

Deleting a merged branch loses nothing. Its commits are part of main's history now; only the sticky note goes. If the branch is not merged yet, git refuses, to protect you.

Practice

If the branches changed different files, or different parts of the same file, git combines them automatically. It stops and asks only when both sides changed the same lines. That is a merge conflict, and it is the next stop.

Keeping a long branch up to date

Working on a branch for a few days while main moves on? Merge main into your branch now and then, so the final merge is small:

$ git switch my-feature
$ git merge main

Same command, opposite direction: now main's new commits flow into your branch.

You want feature's changes in main, and you are currently on feature. What do you run?

Right. Merges go into the branch you are on. git merge main from feature would pull main into feature, which is the opposite direction (useful, just not what was asked).

When does a fast-forward happen?

Right. Nothing to combine, so git only moves the label. No merge commit.

Merge conflicts, calmly

A conflict is not an error, and nothing is broken. It is git saying: two people changed the same lines in different ways, and I refuse to guess which one is right. You decide.

When they happen

You made the salsa mild on main. A friend made it hot on a branch called spicy. You both edited the same line. When you merge, git sees two opinions about one line and stops:

$ git merge spicy
Auto-merging salsa.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in salsa.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

The merge is now paused halfway. git status lists conflicted files as both modified. Everything that merged cleanly is already staged.

Reading the conflict markers

Git writes both versions into the file, fenced off by conflict markers. Hover the parts:

Salsa - 4 ripe tomatoes - 1 onion <<<<<<< HEAD - half a jalapeno (mild) ======= - 3 jalapenos (hot!) >>>>>>> spicy - juice of 1 lime

Hover or tap the marked lines.

Notice line 2 already says "4 ripe tomatoes". Only the spicy branch changed that line, so git merged it without asking. Only the line both sides touched is in conflict.

Fixing it in three steps

  1. Edit the file into its final form. Keep your version, theirs, both, or write something new. Then delete all three marker lines. The file should read like a normal file again.
  2. Stage it with git add salsa.txt. That is how you tell git "this one is resolved".
  3. Finish the merge with git commit. Git already prepared the message.

Editors like VS Code turn step 1 into a click: they highlight each conflict and put buttons above it. This mock works the same way. Resolve both files:

Changed your mind? Abort

$ git merge --abort

Puts everything back exactly the way it was before you ran git merge. Always available while a merge is paused. No harm done.

Now for real

The same conflict in a terminal. You will fix the file in the built-in editor, just as you would with nano or VS Code.

Fewer, smaller conflicts

  • Merge or pull often. The longer two branches drift apart, the bigger the eventual conflict.
  • Keep branches small and short. A two-day branch rarely conflicts badly. A two-month branch always does.
  • Talk to each other. If two people need to rework the same file, coordinate first.
  • Do not reformat whole files in the same commit as real changes. Re-indenting every line makes every line conflict.

Git does not check whether you actually removed the markers. If you git add a file that still contains <<<<<<< lines, they get committed, and your program or document breaks. Always look at the file before adding it.

In a conflict, the lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= are...

Right. HEAD is where you are. The incoming version sits between ======= and >>>>>>>.

You fixed the file and removed the markers. What next?

Right. Adding marks it resolved; committing completes the paused merge.

Rebase (optional, but you will hear about it)

Rebase is the other way to bring branches together. It rewrites your branch so it looks as if you had started from the latest main, giving a perfectly straight history. Powerful, occasionally dangerous, and not required for beginners.

Merge and rebase, side by side

Both tabs start from the same situation: main and feature both have new commits. Step through each and compare the final maps.

Merge shows the truth: two lines that joined. Rebase replays your commits one by one on top of main, producing a straight line. The faded grey stations are the originals.

Rebase creates new commits

This is the key fact. Compare the hashes before and after: they change. A commit's hash depends on its parent, so moving a commit onto a new parent creates a brand-new commit. The old ones still exist for a while (the reflog can find them), but no branch points at them anymore.

The golden rule

If you rebase commits that are already on GitHub and a teammate has pulled them, your history and theirs now disagree about what those commits are. The result is duplicated commits and very confused colleagues. Rebase only your own local work, or a feature branch nobody else uses.

If you rebase your own branch after pushing it, a normal push gets rejected (the histories no longer line up), and you need git push --force-with-lease. Fine on your own branch, a disaster on a shared one.

How to use it

# update your feature branch with the latest main
$ git switch feature
$ git rebase main

If a replayed commit conflicts, git pauses, just like a merge. Fix the file, then:

$ git add salsa.txt
$ git rebase --continue
# or give up and go back to how things were:
$ git rebase --abort

A very common everyday use is git pull --rebase: it puts your unpushed commits on top of what you just downloaded, instead of making a merge commit.

Interactive rebase: tidying up

git rebase -i HEAD~3 opens your last three commits in your editor as a to-do list. The word at the start of each line decides what happens to that commit:

git-rebase-todo
pick   a1b2c3d Add taco recipe
squash e4f5a6b Fix typo in tacos
reword 9c8d7e6 Add salsa to tacos

# pick   = keep the commit as it is
# reword = keep it, but edit its message
# squash = melt it into the commit above
# drop   = delete the commit entirely

Save and close, and git rewrites those commits accordingly. People use it to clean up messy "wip" commits before opening a pull request. The golden rule still applies. (The practice terminals do not simulate interactive rebase.)

So which should I use?

Honest answer: as a beginner, merge. It never rewrites anything, so it is hard to hurt yourself with it. Many teams pick one style per project, and GitHub can enforce it through the merge button (see the pull request stop). When a team asks you to rebase, you now know what that means and what to watch for.

Why do rebased commits get new hashes?

Right. Same changes, different parent, so a different commit. That is also why rebasing shared commits causes trouble.

Is it fine to rebase a branch your teammates are also working on?

Right. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to untangle their copies.

GitHub and remotes

So far everything lived on your computer. Now we connect it to GitHub, so your work is backed up online and other people can download it, add to it and send it back.

What a remote is

A remote is another copy of your repository somewhere else, usually on GitHub. It has its own commits and branches. Your git does not stay in constant contact with it. It only talks to the remote when you tell it to, using three commands:

push

Upload your new commits to the remote.

fetch

Download new commits from the remote, without touching your files or branches.

pull

Fetch, then merge what arrived into the branch you are on.

Step 1: an account and an empty repository

  1. Sign up at github.com. Your username becomes part of every repository URL, so pick one you will still like in five years.
  2. Click the + at the top right, then "New repository".
  3. Name it, for example recipes, and choose Public or Private.
  4. Leave "Add a README", .gitignore and license unticked if you are about to upload an existing project. Otherwise GitHub makes a first commit your project does not have, and your first push gets rejected.
  5. Click "Create repository". GitHub shows a page of setup commands including your repository's URL, like https://github.com/you/recipes.git.

Step 2: connect and push

$ git remote add origin https://github.com/you/recipes.git
$ git push -u origin main
git remote add
Save a remote under a short name.
origin
That name. origin is only a convention for "the main remote"; it could be called anything.
-u
Short for --set-upstream: remember that my local main belongs with origin's main. After doing this once, plain git push and git pull know where to go.
origin main
Where to push (origin) and which branch (main).

The first push asks you to log in, and your GitHub password will not work there. The next stop explains what to do instead.

GitHub's setup page also shows git branch -M main. It renames your current branch to main, for people whose git still starts on master. Harmless if you are already on main.

Or start from GitHub: git clone

If the project already exists on GitHub (yours or anybody's public project), download it with clone. Copy the URL from the green Code button on the repository page:

$ git clone https://github.com/you/recipes.git
Cloning into 'recipes'...
$ cd recipes

Cloning gets you every file, every commit and every branch, and sets up origin automatically. It creates a new folder, so do not forget the cd.

origin/main: your computer's memory of GitHub

After you fetch, pull or push, branches like origin/main show up in the log. These remote-tracking branches are read-only bookmarks meaning "where main was on GitHub last time we talked". They only move when you fetch, pull or push. That is why git status can say "Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'" while GitHub actually has newer commits: git simply has not asked yet.

Step through what happens when a teammate pushes. Watch the dashed origin/main label on your side.

When your push is rejected

$ git push
To https://github.com/you/recipes.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/you/recipes.git'

Normal, and not a problem with your work. GitHub has commits you do not have, because someone pushed since you last pulled. Git refuses to overwrite them. The fix is always the same: git pull (resolving conflicts if any), then git push again.

Do not "fix" a rejected push with git push --force. That replaces GitHub's history with yours and deletes your teammate's commits.

Practice the whole loop

Left graph: your computer. Right graph: GitHub. Push, make a teammate push, then fetch and pull.

Remote commands

git remote -v
List remotes with their URLs
git remote set-url origin URL
Point origin somewhere else, for example after renaming the repository
git push
Upload the current branch to its upstream
git push -u origin name
First push of a new branch
git fetch
Download without touching your work
git pull
Download and merge into the current branch
git branch -a
List local branches plus the origin/ bookmarks

What is the difference between fetch and pull?

Right. Fetch is the safe look-before-you-leap version. Pull is fetch plus merge.

Your push was rejected with "fetch first". What now?

Right. Bring their work in first, then yours can go on top.

Logging in: the easy way, tokens and SSH

The first time you push, git asks who you are, and your GitHub password will not work there (GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for git in 2021). Here are your options, easiest first.

Pick a method

GitHub's own command-line tool, gh, logs you in through your browser and configures git for you. It is also great for pull requests later.

  1. Install it from cli.github.com: an installer on Windows, brew install gh on macOS, or your Linux package manager.
  2. Start the login and answer its questions: GitHub.com, HTTPS, Yes to authenticating git, and "Login with a web browser". 
    $ gh auth login
  3. Copy the one-time code it prints, press Enter, paste the code into the browser page that opens, and click Authorize.
  4. Done. git push now just works. Check any time with gh auth status.

If you installed Git for Windows with the default options, you already have Git Credential Manager. The first time you push, a window opens asking you to sign in to GitHub in your browser. Approve it, and your login is stored securely for next time. Nothing else to do.

On macOS and Linux you can install Git Credential Manager as well (on macOS: brew install --cask git-credential-manager), or simply use the GitHub CLI option.

An SSH key is a pair of files: a private key that never leaves your computer and a public key you hand to GitHub. Think padlock and key: GitHub gets the padlock (public), you keep the key (private), and only your computer can open it. Set it up once and never type a password again.

  1. Generate a key. Press Enter to accept the default file name. Adding a passphrase is a good idea. 
    $ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
  2. Print the public key, the file ending in .pub. Never share the other one. 
    $ cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI... you@example.com
  3. Add it to GitHub: Settings, SSH and GPG keys, New SSH key. Paste it and save.
  4. Test it: 
    $ ssh -T git@github.com
Hi you! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.
  5. Use SSH URLs for your remotes: git@github.com:you/recipes.git instead of the https one.

A personal access token is a long random password that you create on GitHub just for git and other tools. It works with https URLs.

  1. Create one: GitHub, Settings, Developer settings, Personal access tokens, Fine-grained tokens, Generate new token. Give it access to the repositories you need, with "Contents: Read and write".
  2. Copy it right away. GitHub shows it only once.
  3. When git asks for your password, paste the token. The username is still your GitHub username.

Treat it exactly like a password: never commit it, never paste it into chats. Tokens expire, so set yourself a reminder.

HTTPS or SSH URLs?

HTTPS

https://github.com/you/recipes.git

Works everywhere, even behind strict company firewalls. Pairs with the GitHub CLI, the browser popup or a token.

SSH

git@github.com:you/recipes.git

Needs the key setup, then never asks again. Some networks block it.

You can switch an existing repository between them at any time:

$ git remote set-url origin git@github.com:you/recipes.git

Error messages, translated

Authentication failed
You typed your account password. Use one of the methods above instead.
Permission denied (publickey)
The SSH key is missing, not added to GitHub, or not the right one. ssh -T git@github.com tests it.
Repository not found
A typo in the URL, a private repository you are not logged in for, or you are logged in as a different account. GitHub says "not found" instead of "forbidden" on purpose, so private repositories stay secret.
Permission to X denied to Y
You are logged in fine, but your account may not push there. Ask to be added as a collaborator, or fork the project.

Which file of an SSH key pair do you give to GitHub?

Right. The public key is the padlock; anyone may have it. The private key never leaves your computer.

Pull requests

This is how teams really work together on GitHub. Nobody pushes straight to main. You push a branch and open a pull request: a proposal saying "please review these changes and merge them in".

What a pull request is

A pull request (PR) is a page on GitHub attached to a branch. It shows every commit and every changed line, has a discussion thread, runs automatic tests, and ends with a Merge button. The name comes from asking the maintainers to pull your changes in. GitLab calls the same thing a merge request.

Why not merge on your own computer and push? Because a pull request gives you:

  • Review: a teammate reads your change before it lands. Bugs get caught and knowledge spreads.
  • Automatic checks: tests run on every push, so a broken change shows a red X before it is merged.
  • A record: months later, the PR explains why a change was made, with the whole discussion attached.
  • A protected main: repositories can require a PR and an approval for every change to main.

The workflow

  1. Update main: git switch main, then git pull
  2. Branch: git switch -c add-tacos
  3. Work and commit, as many commits as you like
  4. Push the branch: git push -u origin add-tacos
  5. Open the pull request on GitHub
  6. Discuss, review, fix: push more commits to the same branch; the PR updates itself
  7. Merge once it is approved and the checks are green
  8. Clean up: delete the branch, then git switch main and git pull

Walk through one

A simplified mock of the GitHub pages involved. Click the pulsing buttons inside the fake browser, or use Next.

Three ways to merge

GitHub's merge button has a dropdown with three options. Here is what each does to main on GitHub, for a pull request with two commits:

Merge commit
Keeps every commit, plus a merge commit. Complete, but busy.
Squash and merge
One commit per pull request. The most popular choice for tidy history; your "fix typo" commits never reach main.
Rebase and merge
Keeps every commit, in a straight line, without a merge commit.

Squashing creates a brand-new commit, so git on your computer does not recognize your branch as merged, and git branch -d add-tacos complains that it is not fully merged. If you know the PR was merged, git branch -D add-tacos is fine.

Writing a good pull request

  • Keep it small. A 50-line PR gets a careful review in ten minutes. A 2,000-line PR gets "looks good to me" and a hidden bug.
  • A title that says what it does: "Add taco recipe", not "Updates".
  • A description that says why, how to test it, and screenshots for anything visual.
  • Link the issue: Closes #12 in the description closes issue 12 automatically when the PR is merged.
  • Draft PRs (the arrow next to "Create pull request") mean "not ready, but have a look". Great for early feedback.

Reviewing someone else's

  • Open Files changed, and click the + beside any line to comment on it.
  • Use suggestions for small fixes; the author can apply them with a click.
  • Finish with Comment, Approve or Request changes.
  • Be specific and kind. Comment on the code, not the person. Questions ("what happens if the list is empty?") land better than verdicts.

The same thing from the terminal

With the GitHub CLI you never leave the terminal. Do the full cycle here, including merging on the pretend GitHub:

A reviewer asks for a change on your pull request. What do you do?

Right. A pull request follows its branch. New commits on the branch appear in the PR automatically.

Your PR was merged on GitHub. Why doesn't your local main have the change?

Right. git switch main and git pull bring the merged result down.

Forks and open source

You can read any public repository, but you cannot push to other people's projects. To contribute anyway, you fork: make your own copy on GitHub, change that, and send a pull request back to the original.

Fork, clone, branch: not the same thing

WordMakes a copy whereUse it when
BranchInside the same repositoryYou can push there and want to work on something separately
CloneOn your computerYou want to work on any repository locally
ForkOn GitHub, under your accountYou want to change a project you cannot push to

How the pieces connect

  1. Fork: click Fork on the project's GitHub page. You now own you/cookbook.
  2. Clone your fork: git clone https://github.com/you/cookbook.git. Your fork becomes origin.
  3. Branch and commit as usual.
  4. Push to your fork: git push -u origin my-fix.
  5. Open a pull request: GitHub offers to open it against the original project, and its maintainers review it like any other PR.

Staying in sync with the original

While you work, the original project moves on, and your fork does not update itself. Add the original as a second remote, traditionally called upstream, and bring its changes in:

$ git remote add upstream https://github.com/open-kitchen/cookbook.git
$ git fetch upstream
$ git switch main
$ git merge upstream/main
$ git push origin main

Or click Sync fork on your fork's GitHub page, then git pull locally. Same result.

Contributing without embarrassment

  • Read CONTRIBUTING.md first. Most projects explain their rules, style and how to run the tests.
  • Look for issues labeled good first issue or help wanted. They are picked for newcomers.
  • Comment on the issue before big work, so two people do not solve the same thing.
  • Keep the pull request focused on one thing. Do not reformat the whole project on the way.
  • Be patient. Maintainers are often volunteers. A polite nudge after a week is fine.
  • Documentation fixes count. Clarifying a confusing README is a perfect first contribution.

You forked a project and cloned your fork. What is origin?

Right. origin is wherever you cloned from. The original project is the one you add as upstream.

The rest of GitHub

GitHub is more than a place to push. A quick tour of the features you will bump into: READMEs, issues, releases, Actions, Pages, and the settings that protect your main branch.

The repository page

Code
Files, the branch dropdown (top left), commit history (the clock icon), and the green Code button with the clone URL.
Issues
Bug reports, ideas and to-dos, each with its own discussion.
Pull requests
Open and past pull requests.
Actions
Automation runs, such as tests and deployments.
Settings
Collaborators, branch protection, Pages, secrets. Only visible with admin rights.

At the top: Star (a public bookmark, and a thank-you to the authors), Watch (notifications) and Fork.

Press . (the period key) on any repository page on github.com to open it in a full VS Code editor in your browser. Press t to search files by name.

README.md and Markdown

A file named README.md at the top of your repository is shown as the project's front page. The .md stands for Markdown: plain text with a few symbols for formatting. The same syntax works in issues, pull request descriptions and comments. Edit the left side:

You typeYou get
# Title, ## SectionHeadings
**bold**, *italic*bold, italic
- item or 1. itemA bulleted or numbered list
- [ ] taskA checkbox (clickable in issues and pull requests)
`code`Inline code
[text](https://...)A link
> quoteA quote block

A good README answers what the project is, how to install or run it, and how to contribute.

Issues

Issues are a project's to-do list and bug tracker. Each has a number (#12), a discussion, labels like bug or good first issue, and assignees. Mention one anywhere by typing #12. Write Closes #12 in a pull request description and the issue closes itself when the PR is merged.

A useful bug report says what you did, what you expected, what happened instead, and which versions you use. Screenshots help enormously.

Releases

A release is a named version of your project, like v1.2.0, with notes about what changed and files to download. It is built on a git tag. Create one from Releases, Draft a new release on the repository page; GitHub can even write the notes from your merged pull requests.

GitHub Actions: the green check

GitHub Actions runs scripts automatically when something happens. The classic example: run the tests on every push and pull request. That is where the green checkmark or red X on commits and PRs comes from, a practice called CI. A workflow is a small YAML file in .github/workflows/:

.github/workflows/test.yml
name: test
on: [push, pull_request]        # when to run
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest      # a fresh virtual machine
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4   # get the code
      - run: npm install            # install dependencies
      - run: npm test               # run the tests

You do not have to write these on day one. Just know what the checks on your pull request are, and click Details next to a red X to see what failed.

GitHub Pages: free website hosting

A repository of HTML files can be published as a website for free: Settings, Pages, pick the branch, and it appears at https://you.github.io/repository-name. Perfect for portfolios, documentation and small projects. A standalone HTML file like this guide would work there as-is.

Protecting main

Under Settings, Rules (or Branches), admins can protect main: require a pull request for every change, require approvals and passing checks, and block force pushes. That is why the Merge button in the pull request walkthrough stayed locked until someone approved.

Other things you will run into

LICENSE
States what others may legally do with your code. No license means nobody else may reuse it. choosealicense.com helps you pick.
.github/
Templates for issues and pull requests, workflows, and CODEOWNERS (who must review which files).
Gists
gist.github.com, for sharing a single snippet quickly. Each gist is secretly a tiny git repository.
Discussions
A forum tab for questions that are not bugs.
Security tab
Dependabot alerts about vulnerable libraries, with automatic pull requests that update them.

Where does the green checkmark next to a commit usually come from?

Right. Checks are automated. Approvals are shown separately on the pull request.

Undo (almost) anything

Once something is committed, it is very hard to lose it for good. This stop is your emergency manual: pick your situation, get the exact commands, and know which undos are harmless and which are not.

Oh no. What happened?

Pick a situation. The color says how risky the fix is: green is safe, amber rewrites history (fine for commits only you have), red can throw work away.

The golden rule of undoing

A commit that exists only on your computer can be rewritten freely: amend it, reset it, rebase it. Once it is pushed and others may have it, do not rewrite it. Use git revert instead, which undoes it with a new commit.

reset: moving the branch backwards

Reset moves your current branch back to an earlier commit. The mode decides what happens to the changes from the commits you stepped back over. Try all three tabs and watch the areas panel:

ModeBranch moves backStaging areaYour files
--softYesChanges stay stagedUntouched
--mixed (default)YesUnstagedUntouched, the changes are still there
--hardYesClearedReset too. Uncommitted work is gone.

revert: undoing in public

Revert removes nothing. It creates a new commit that does the exact opposite of an old one. History stays intact, so it is safe on shared branches.

amend: fixing the last commit

A typo in the message, or a forgotten file? git commit --amend replaces the last commit with a corrected one. It is a new commit with a new hash, so only amend before pushing.

reflog: the safety net under the safety net

Git privately writes down every place HEAD has been, in the reflog. Reset too far? Deleted a branch? Botched a rebase? The commits are almost certainly still there, and the reflog tells you their hashes:

$ git reflog
44fd3dc (HEAD -> main) HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
06314b3 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add taco recipe
44fd3dc HEAD@{2}: commit: Add salsa
$ git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
HEAD is now at 06314b3 Add taco recipe

Reflog entries are kept for about three months, and commits nothing points to survive at least a couple of weeks. The reflog is local: it only knows what happened on this computer.

Changes that were never committed. If you git restore a file, or git reset --hard or git clean away uncommitted edits, git never had a copy of them. That is the real reason to commit often: every commit is a save point you can always return to.

Practice: fix a messy repository

You pushed a bad commit to main, and your team already pulled it. How do you undo it?

Right. Revert adds a new commit that everyone can simply pull. Resetting and force pushing would rip the commit out from under your team.

Which reset mode can permanently destroy uncommitted changes?

Right. --hard overwrites your files. The other two only move the branch and the staging area.

Stash, tags and power tools

Smaller commands that make daily life easier: parking half-done work, marking releases, copying single commits, and finding out who changed a line and when.

git stash: park your work

You are halfway through something when an urgent fix comes in, and git will not let you switch branches with conflicting uncommitted changes. Stash puts them in a drawer and hands you a clean folder:

$ git stash
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: 3a1f2c9 Raise coffee price
# ...switch branches, fix the urgent thing, come back...
$ git stash pop
git stash
Park all changes to tracked files
git stash -u
Also park brand-new, untracked files
git stash push -m "note"
Park with a description
git stash list
See what is in the drawer
git stash pop
Take the newest one out and apply it
git stash apply
Apply it, but keep a copy in the drawer
git stash drop
Throw the newest one away

Stashes are easy to forget about. If you will be away from the work for more than an hour, a quick commit on a branch ("wip: halfway through the menu") is often safer. You can tidy it up later.

Tags: naming a release

A tag is a permanent label on one commit, usually a version number. Unlike a branch, it never moves.

$ git tag v1.0.0
$ git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "Adds dark mode"
$ git push origin --tags

Tags are not pushed automatically, so remember the last line. -a makes an annotated tag with a message and an author, which is what releases should use.

Most projects use semantic versioning, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump PATCH for bug fixes (1.0.1), MINOR for new features that break nothing (1.1.0), and MAJOR when you break compatibility (2.0.0).

cherry-pick: copy one commit

Need one specific commit from another branch, but not the rest? Cherry-pick copies just that commit onto your current branch.

blame: who wrote this line?

$ git blame menu.txt
a4c1e20 (You 2026-09-14  1) Menu
9f3b7d1 (Sam 2026-09-15  2) Coffee 3.20
a4c1e20 (You 2026-09-14  3) Tea 2.50

For every line: the commit that last changed it, who made it and when. Then git show 9f3b7d1 tells you why. Despite the name, blame is for understanding code, not for pointing fingers. GitHub has a Blame button on every file too.

bisect: finding the commit that broke it

Something worked last month and is broken now, with 200 commits in between. git bisect runs a binary search: it checks out the commit halfway, you say good or bad, it halves again. You find the culprit in about 8 steps instead of 200.

$ git bisect start
$ git bisect bad              # the current version is broken
$ git bisect good v1.0.0      # this old version worked
# git checks out a commit in the middle. Test it, then:
$ git bisect good             # or: git bisect bad
# ...repeat until git names the first bad commit...
$ git bisect reset            # back to where you started

Aliases: shorter commands

Tired of typing? Make your own shortcuts:

$ git config --global alias.st status
$ git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --all"
$ git st
$ git lg

Aliases work in the practice terminals too.

Practice

What is the difference between a tag and a branch?

Right. That is why tags are used for versions: v1.0.0 should always mean exactly the same code.

Good habits and team workflows

The commands are the easy part. What separates a painless project from a miserable one is a handful of habits. None of them are hard, and all of them pay off.

Commit small, commit often

A commit should be one logical change: "Add search box", not "Monday's work". Small commits are easy to review, easy to revert and easy to understand later. Committing often means you always have a recent save point, which makes undoing cheap.

Write messages future you can use

Type a message and watch the signal. It checks the conventions most projects follow.

  • First line: a short summary in the command form, about 50 characters, no period. Test it by reading "If applied, this commit will fix crash when the cart is empty".
  • Need more room? Leave a blank line and explain why in as much detail as you like. From the terminal: git commit -m "Title" -m "Longer explanation".
  • Some teams use Conventional Commits prefixes: feat: add search, fix: handle empty cart, docs: update README. Copy whatever the project already does.

The GitHub flow

The simple workflow most teams use, and what this whole guide has been building towards:

  1. main always works. Nobody commits half-finished work to it directly.
  2. Every task gets a branch, created from an up-to-date main.
  3. Push early and open a pull request (a draft is fine) to get feedback.
  4. Review, then merge once the checks are green.
  5. Delete the branch and start the next task from a fresh main.

Rules that prevent disasters

  • Pull before you start working, and before you push. Fewer surprises, smaller conflicts.
  • Look before you commit: git status and git diff --staged catch the stray debug file.
  • Never commit secrets. Set up .gitignore on day one.
  • Never force-push a shared branch. On your own branch, prefer --force-with-lease, which refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.
  • Read commands from the internet before running them, especially anything containing --force, reset --hard or clean.
  • Keep branches short-lived. Days, not months.

Things that bite people eventually

Line endings
Windows ends lines with two invisible characters, macOS and Linux with one. Mixed teams see whole files as "changed". Set core.autocrlf as shown in setup, or add a .gitattributes file containing * text=auto.
Big files
GitHub rejects files over 100 MB and warns above 50 MB. For large assets use Git LFS (git lfs track "*.psd"), or keep them out of git altogether.
Case-only renames
Renaming Readme.md to README.md confuses git on Windows and macOS. Use git mv Readme.md README.md.
Empty folders
Git only tracks files, so an empty folder is invisible to it. Put a placeholder file inside (often named .gitkeep) if the folder must exist.

Apps and buttons are fine

VS Code's Source Control panel, GitHub Desktop, JetBrains IDEs, lazygit, Fork, Sublime Merge: all excellent, and many professionals live in them. Now that you know the commands, every button makes sense: Stage is git add, Sync is pull and then push, Discard is git restore. Use whatever is fastest, and drop to the terminal when something looks off.

Which is the best commit message?

Right. Specific, short, in the command form, no period. You could find this commit a year from now.

Final challenge

One last mission that strings everything together in the order it happens in real life. After that, a sandbox with no rules, and pointers for where to go next.

The graduation mission

Sam started a shared cookbook on GitHub and gave you access. You will clone it, change the menu and push. Except Sam is editing the very same line at the very same time. You will need clone, commit, push, pull, conflict resolution and push again.

Sandbox

Anything goes. Two GitHub repositories exist here: an empty one at https://github.com/you/sandbox.git, and Sam's cookbook to clone. Type help for the command list, sim teammate to make a teammate push, and borrow ideas from the cheat sheet.

Things to try in the sandbox

  • Create a project and push it to the empty sandbox repository with git remote add and git push -u.
  • Make several branches, merge them in different orders, and watch the map.
  • Cause a conflict on purpose. Back out with git merge --abort the first time, then resolve it properly.
  • Rebase a branch, then find the old commits with git reflog.
  • Delete the .git folder with rm -rf .git and see what is left. Only in here, please.

Where to go from here

  • Use it for real. Put your next project, your notes or your config files under git and push them to GitHub. Daily use is what makes it stick.
  • Contribute one small thing to an open source project. A typo fix in documentation is a perfectly respectable first pull request.
  • Read Pro Git, the free official book, when you want every detail.
  • GitHub Docs cover every button on the website.
  • When stuck: git status first, then the Undo stop.
